paper_b.title: A Short Introduction to Boosting (Freund & Schapire 1999)

metadata.description: Both papers describe iterative multiplicative-style updates that achieve no-regret/exponentially-vanishing-error guarantees: paper A (Hart-Mas-Colell) is the game-theoretic regret-matching/regret-based dynamics line, while paper B (Freund-Schapire) is the boosting/AdaBoost line. AdaBoost's exponential reweighting on misclassified examples and Hart-Mas-Colell's gradient-of-potential reweighting on positive-regret actions are parallel rediscoveries of the multiplicative-weights / no-regret idea in distinct communities (machine learning vs game theory); paper B explicitly notes the game-theoretic interpretation in remark RP279.3. Note: both extractions are PDF-fallbacks with reduced math fidelity, and both have registry-mismatch notes; the alignment is based on the ACTUAL PDF contents.

matches.explanation: Paper A's regret-based ($P^i$-)strategy plays $q^i = \widehat{\nabla} P^i(D^i(z))$ -- a normalized gradient of a potential evaluated at the regret vector, with regret-matching the special case $P(x) = \|[x]_+\|_2^2$. Paper B's AdaBoost iteratively updates a distribution $D_t$ over training examples and aggregates weak hypotheses. Both are no-regret-flavored iterative procedures whose update direction is set by the current 'badness' vector (regrets in A; weighted errors in B). They are not the same algorithm (regret-matching has linear-in-regret weights; AdaBoost has exponential-in-margin weights, i.e. the entropy-potential MWU instance), so this is analogous rather than exact.

Both pairs encode the per-round 'badness' signal that drives the update. Paper A's regret vector $D^i_k(z) = u^i(k, z^{-i}) - u^i(z)$ measures how much player $i$ would gain by always playing action $k$, and the normalized gradient $\widehat{
abla} P$ converts it into a play distribution. Paper B's weak-hypothesis error $\epsilon_t = \Pr_{i \sim D_t}[h_t(x_i) 
e y_i] = \sum_{i: h_t(x_i) 
e y_i} D_t(i)$ measures the hypothesis's loss against the current distribution. The roles match (input to the update rule that defines the next mixed/example-distribution) but the formulations differ (action-regret vs example-error).

Paper A's ODE $\dot z = (q - z)/t$ with $q = \widehat{\nabla} P(D)$ describes the continuous-time multiplicative-style update of the play distribution. Paper B's $D_{t+1}(i) = D_t(i) \exp(-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i))/Z_t$ (with $D_1(i) = 1/m$) is the canonical multiplicative-weights update on training examples. Both reweight a probability distribution by the local performance of a deterministic 'choice' (action vs hypothesis), with normalization. The continuous-time/discrete-time and action-space/example-space distinction makes this analogous; the underlying multiplicative-weights mechanism is the same.

Paper A's Theorem 3.1 says regret-based play drives every component of the regret vector to be at most zero in the limit ($\lim_t D^i_k(z(t)) \le 0$). Paper B's training-error theorem gives $\Pr[H(x) \ne y] \le \prod_t \sqrt{1 - 4 \gamma_t^2} \le \exp(-2 \sum_t \gamma_t^2)$, i.e. exponential decay of the misclassification rate. Both are the 'main convergence guarantee' of the corresponding iterative no-regret/boosting algorithm: regrets vanish in A, training error vanishes (with quantitative rate) in B. Conceptually parallel; the bounds are stated in different units (asymptotic vs explicit rate) and are not formally equivalent.

Paper A's proof of Theorem 3.1 is a Lyapunov argument: $\pi^i := P^i(D^i(z))$ is a strict Lyapunov function, $\dot \pi^i = -\nabla P^i(D^i) \cdot D^i < 0$. Paper B's training-error bound is proved (in the underlying Freund-Schapire 1997 paper, summarized here in EP279.5) by tracking the product of normalizers $Z_t = 2\sqrt{\epsilon_t(1-\epsilon_t)}$ -- an exact-potential / multiplicative-Lyapunov argument. Both proofs use a one-line 'potential decreases' computation along the dynamics. Confidence dropped to medium because paper B's PDF-fallback extraction does not break out the proof as a separate node.

Corollary 3.2 says joint regret-based play converges to the Hannan set $H = \{D^i(z) \le 0 \, \forall i\}$, i.e. to a no-regret outcome. The boosting analog is that AdaBoost (with sufficient weak edges) drives training error to zero exponentially fast (EP279.5), i.e. converges to perfect agreement on the training set. Both are 'in the limit, the algorithm achieves the best one could hope for against the seen data', from regret-matching and from boosting respectively. Different objects (Hannan set vs zero-error classifier), parallel role.

The Hannan set -- joint distributions with non-positive regret -- is the game-theoretic limiting object of paper A. Paper B has no explicit 'set of equilibria' analog; its limiting object is a low-error classifier, not a polytope of distributions. No counterpart.

Strategic-form $N$-person game is the basic object of paper A's setting. Paper B is set in supervised binary classification ($X \to \{-1,+1\}$) with no game-theoretic apparatus; the gambler/horse-racing example (ExP279.1) is metaphor only.
Mixed actions and joint distributions over action profiles have no analog in paper B's classification setup. Paper B's 'distribution' $D_t$ is over training examples (a different role).

The abstract potential class $P$ on $\mathbb{R}^m$ with axioms (P1)-(P4) (smoothness, vanishing on the negative orthant, controlled scaling) is paper A's central abstraction. Paper B uses a specific exponential potential implicitly (through $Z_t$) but does not formalize a class of potentials -- so this paper-A definition has no Level-1 counterpart in paper B.

Conditional regret $C^i_{jk}$, correlated equilibrium, and conditional regret-based strategies are paper A's apparatus for the correlated-equilibrium convergence (Section 5). Paper B has no analog of conditional regrets / correlated equilibrium -- boosting is not multi-player and the recommendation-conditional structure does not arise.

Convergence to Nash equilibria in two-person zero-sum games. The closest boosting analog is the LP/zero-sum-game formulation of boosting noted in RP279.3, but paper B does not state a Nash-convergence theorem; this paper-A theorem has no L1 counterpart in paper B.
Convergence to Nash in two-person potential games (Theorem 4.4 and Corollary 4.6) is a paper A new result with no boosting counterpart.
Vanishing conditional regret and convergence to correlated equilibria are paper A specific (Section 5); boosting does not produce or use correlated-equilibrium-type guarantees.
Discrete-time Nash convergence in two-person potential games is a paper A appendix-A new result; no analog in paper B.
Continuous-time generalized Blackwell approachability (Appendix C). Paper B does not use approachability.
Persistence of positive regret (Lemma 3.3). No boosting analog: in AdaBoost the per-example weights can shrink to zero on easy examples.
Hannan-set + product-payoff implies Nash (Lemma 4.1). Game-theoretic; no boosting analog.
Coordinate bound by potential (Lemma 4.3). Auxiliary analytic lemma for paper A; no boosting analog.
Lemma 4.5 / Lemma A.2 (a Lipschitz integrable function / a slowly-varying integrable sequence vanishes). Standard analysis lemmas internal to paper A's convergence proofs, with no role in paper B.
Continuity bound for two stochastic ODEs (Lemma B.3, Gronwall-type). Internal lemma for paper A's appendix B; no analog in paper B.

Continuous-time Markov ODE results in Appendix B ($\dot x \to 0$ for slowly-varying stochastic $A(t)$; uniform $1/\sqrt t$ bound on $e^{t(A-I)}(A-I)$). Internal analytic propositions for paper A; no analog in paper B.
Proof of Lemma 3.3. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of Lemma 4.1. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of zero-sum convergence theorem (TP278.2). No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of Lemma 4.3. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of Theorem 4.4 (Lyapunov $v$ for two-person potential games). No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of Lemma 4.5. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of Corollary 4.6. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of conditional-regret theorem (TP278.4). No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of discrete-time Nash convergence (Theorem A.1). No counterpart in paper B.
Proofs of analytic Lemma A.2 / Propositions B.1, B.2 / Lemma B.3. Internal to paper A's proofs of the discrete-time and Markov-ODE results; no counterpart in paper B.
Proof of generalized approachability (Theorem C.1). No counterpart in paper B.
AdaBoost.M1 and AdaBoost.M2/MR are paper-B's multiclass extensions of binary AdaBoost. Paper A is single-classification-task-free and has no multiclass analog.
Margin theory (margin of an example, margin formula, margin-based generalization bound). Specific to boosting/large-margin classification; paper A has no margin notion.
Instance/weight vectors and the $\ell_1/\ell_\infty$ vs $\ell_2/\ell_2$ max-min-margin objective relating AdaBoost to SVMs. Paper A has no SVM connection or norm-based margin formulation.

AdaBoost's exponential-weights coefficient $\alpha_t = \tfrac12 \ln((1-\epsilon_t)/\epsilon_t)$ is the entropy-potential MWU instance; paper A's regret-matching uses $P(x) = \|[x]_+\|_2^2$ (quadratic potential), so there is no node-level analog for this specific log-odds formula.

Final hypothesis $H(x) = \mathrm{sign}(\sum_t \alpha_t h_t(x))$ is boosting-specific (sign of a weighted vote). Paper A's output is a play distribution / time-average $z(t)$, not an aggregated classifier.
VC-style generalization-error bound $\widehat\Pr + \tilde O(\sqrt{Td/m})$. Generalization theory is paper-B specific; paper A has no out-of-sample / generalization analysis.
